questions.question: Q1. Define work. State when work is done.
questions.answer: Work is done when a force displaces a body in its direction: W = F·s = Fscosθ. Work is zero if there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
questions.shortcut: W = Fscosθ; θ=90° → W=0; θ=0 → W=Fs.
questions.example: Holding a 10 kg bag still (no displacement) → zero work.

questions.question: Q2. Find work done by a 20 N force moving a block 5 m at 30° to the displacement.
questions.shortcut: Use the component of F along displacement.

questions.question: Q3. Explain work done by a variable force.
questions.answer: For a variable force, work is the integral W = ∫ F dx over the path; graphically it equals the area under the F–x curve.
questions.example: Spring: W = ½kx² comes from ∫kx dx.

questions.question: Q4. Why is work a scalar though force and displacement are vectors?
questions.answer: Work is a scalar because it is the dot product of force and displacement: W = F·s = Fscosθ, which has magnitude only, no direction (it can be positive, negative or zero). ▥ 5.1 Work Done  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Sign of Work: Chart by Angle ▣ 5.2 Power
questions.example: Lifting does positive work, friction does negative work.

questions.question: Q5. Define power and give its SI unit.
questions.answer: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t. Instantaneous power P = F·v. SI unit = watt (1 W = 1 J/s).
questions.example: Lifting 100 J in 2 s → P = 50 W.

questions.question: Q6. A crane lifts 500 kg through 4 m in 10 s. Find its power.
Q7. Two people climb the same staircase; who does more work and who has greater power?
questions.answer: The heavier person does more work (more mgh). The one who takes less time has greater power (P = W/t), whether he is lighter or heavier. ▥ 5.2 Power  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Average vs Instantaneous Power ▣ 5.3 Work-Energy Theorem & KE/PE
questions.shortcut: More mass → more work; less time → more power.
questions.example: A slow heavy climber has high work but low power.

questions.question: Q8. State and prove the work-energy theorem.
questions.answer: The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ½mv² − ½mu². From F=ma and s=(v²−u²)/2a, F·s = ma·(v²−u²)/2a = ½m(v²−u²).
questions.example: A 2 kg body speeds up 3→5 m/s → ΔKE = 16 J of work.

questions.question: Q9. Define kinetic and potential energy with examples.
questions.answer: KE = ½mv² (energy of motion), e.g. a moving car. PE = mgh (gravitational, energy of position), e.g. water behind a dam; also ½kx² for a spring.
questions.example: A swinging pendulum trades PE and KE.

questions.question: Q10. A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes to rest. Find work done by the brakes.
questions.answer: W = ΔKE = 0 − ½(1000)(400) = −200000 J. The brakes do 2×10⁵ J of (negative) work, removed as heat. ▥ 5.3 Work-Energy Theorem & KE/PE  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Kinetic Energy vs Potential Energy ▣ 5.4 Conservation of Energy

questions.question: Q11. State the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it changes form. Total energy of an isolated system remains constant: KE + PE = constant (when only conservative forces act).
questions.shortcut: Top: PE max, KE=0. Bottom: KE max, PE=0. Total constant.
questions.example: A falling object: mgh at top = ½mv² at bottom.

questions.question: Q12. Find the speed of a body falling from 80 m (from rest).
Q13. Explain energy changes in a simple pendulum.
questions.answer: At the extreme positions height (and PE) is maximum and speed (KE) is zero; at the lowest point KE is maximum and PE is minimum. Total mechanical energy stays constant (ignoring air resistance). ▥ 5.4 Conservation of Energy  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Mechanical Energy: When Is it Conserved? ▣ 5.5 Conservative & Non-conservative Forces; Collisions
questions.example: Swing is fastest at the bottom.

questions.question: Q14. Define conservative and non-conservative forces with examples.
questions.answer: Conservative forces: work is path-independent and total work around a closed loop is zero (gravity, spring, electrostatic). Non-conservative: work depends on path, converts energy to other forms (friction, air resistance).
questions.example: Sliding down a rough incline loses mechanical energy to heat.

questions.question: Q15. Distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions.
questions.answer: Elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved (e.g. ideal gas molecules). Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved but KE is not (part converts to heat/sound); perfectly inelastic bodies stick together.
questions.shortcut: Elastic: KE conserved. Inelastic: KE lost. Momentum conserved in both.
questions.example: Billiard balls ≈ elastic; car crashes are inelastic.

questions.question: Q16. In a perfectly inelastic collision, is momentum or kinetic energy conserved?
questions.answer: Momentum is conserved (no external force). Kinetic energy is not conserved; some is converted to heat, sound and deformation. The bodies move with a common final velocity.
questions.example: Two clay balls stick together and slow down.

questions.question: Q17. Coefficient of restitution e. What is e for elastic and perfectly inelastic collision?
questions.answer: e = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach. For an elastic collision e = 1; for a perfectly inelastic collision (bodies stick) e = 0. ▥ 5.5 Conservative & Non-conservative Forces; Collisions  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Elastic vs Inelastic Collision PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: e=1 elastic; e=0 perfectly inelastic; 0<e<1 partially.
questions.example: Rubber ball has higher e than a clay ball.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the work-energy theorem.
theoryItems.answer: Net work = ma×s = ma(v²−u²)/2a = ½m(v²−u²) = ΔKE. So W_net = change in kinetic energy, regardless of the forces involved.
theoryItems.example: A force speeding a body up stores the work as KE.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the energy stored in a stretched spring (elastic potential energy).
theoryItems.answer: Work = area under the F–x graph; for Hooke's law F = kx this is a triangle: U = ½·F·Δx = ½kx². Energy density = ½(stress)(strain).
theoryItems.example: A 100 N over 0.1 m stores 5 J.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. Define work, kinetic energy and potential energy with units.
theoryItems.answer: Work = force × displacement along the force (J). KE = ½mv² (J) – energy of motion. PE (grav) = mgh (J) – energy of position. All in joules.
theoryItems.example: A lifted 10 kg at 2 m → PE = 196 J.

theoryItems.question: [State] T4. State the law of conservation of energy and apply it to a falling body.
theoryItems.answer: Energy is neither created nor destroyed; it changes form. A body falling from rest: mgh at the top = ½mv² at the bottom, so v = √(2gh).

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T5. Compare elastic and inelastic collisions (with coefficient of restitution).
theoryItems.answer: Elastic: both momentum and KE conserved, e = 1 (ideal gas, billiard). Inelastic: momentum conserved but KE lost, e < 1; perfectly inelastic (bodies stick), e = 0, maximum KE lost.
theoryItems.example: Car crash = inelastic; pool balls ≈ elastic.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the work-energy theorem's application in braking.
theoryItems.answer: The braking (friction) force does negative work equal to the loss in KE: W = −½mv². The work dissipated is converted to heat in the brakes; this fixes the minimum stopping distance.
theoryItems.example: Stopping a car converts KE into thermal energy.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain conservative and non-conservative forces with examples.
theoryItems.answer: Conservative (gravity, spring, electrostatic): work depends only on end points, zero around a closed loop, and a potential energy can be defined. Non-conservative (friction, air drag): work depends on path, converts mechanical energy to heat, no potential energy.
theoryItems.example: Sliding down a rough ramp loses energy to heat.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T8. Why is the total energy of a bound system negative?
theoryItems.answer: Because zero energy is set at infinite separation; since binding holds the system together, its total energy lies below that zero, i.e. negative. Unbound systems have E ≥ 0.
theoryItems.example: A satellite in orbit has negative total energy.

▣ 5.1 Work Done
Q1. Define work. State when work is done.
Answer:  Work is done when a force displaces a body in its direction: W = F·s = Fscosθ. Work is zero if there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
⚡ Shortcut:  W = Fscosθ; θ=90° → W=0; θ=0 → W=Fs.
Example:  Holding a 10 kg bag still (no displacement) → zero work.
Q2. Find work done by a 20 N force moving a block 5 m at 30° to the displacement.
⚡ Shortcut:  Use the component of F along displacement.
Example:  ≈ 87 J of positive work.
Q3. Explain work done by a variable force.
Answer:  For a variable force, work is the integral W = ∫ F dx over the path; graphically it equals the area under the F–x curve.
⚡ Shortcut:  W = area under F–x graph.
Example:  Spring: W = ½kx² comes from ∫kx dx.
Q4. Why is work a scalar though force and displacement are vectors?
Answer:  Work is a scalar because it is the dot product of force and displacement: W = F·s = Fscosθ, which has magnitude only, no direction (it can be positive, negative or zero).
⚡ Shortcut:  Dot product → scalar.
Example:  Lifting does positive work, friction does negative work.
▥ 5.1 Work Done  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Sign of Work: Chart by Angle
▣ 5.2 Power
Q5. Define power and give its SI unit.
Answer:  Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t. Instantaneous power P = F·v. SI unit = watt (1 W = 1 J/s).
⚡ Shortcut:  P = W/t or P = Fv.
Example:  Lifting 100 J in 2 s → P = 50 W.
Q6. A crane lifts 500 kg through 4 m in 10 s. Find its power.
⚡ Shortcut:  P = mgh/t.
Example:  ≈ 1.96 kW.
Q7. Two people climb the same staircase; who does more work and who has greater power?
Answer:  The heavier person does more work (more mgh). The one who takes less time has greater power (P = W/t), whether he is lighter or heavier.
⚡ Shortcut:  More mass → more work; less time → more power.
Example:  A slow heavy climber has high work but low power.
▥ 5.2 Power  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Average vs Instantaneous Power
▣ 5.3 Work-Energy Theorem & KE/PE
Q8. State and prove the work-energy theorem.
Answer:  The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ½mv² − ½mu². From F=ma and s=(v²−u²)/2a, F·s = ma·(v²−u²)/2a = ½m(v²−u²).
⚡ Shortcut:  W_net = ΔKE = ½m(v²−u²).
Example:  A 2 kg body speeds up 3→5 m/s → ΔKE = 16 J of work.
Q9. Define kinetic and potential energy with examples.
Answer:  KE = ½mv² (energy of motion), e.g. a moving car. PE = mgh (gravitational, energy of position), e.g. water behind a dam; also ½kx² for a spring.
⚡ Shortcut:  KE=½mv²; PE=mgh or ½kx².
Example:  A swinging pendulum trades PE and KE.
Q10. A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes to rest. Find work done by the brakes.
Answer:  W = ΔKE = 0 − ½(1000)(400) = −200000 J. The brakes do 2×10⁵ J of (negative) work, removed as heat.
⚡ Shortcut:  Work to stop = initial KE.
Example:  200 kJ dissipated.
▥ 5.3 Work-Energy Theorem & KE/PE  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Kinetic Energy vs Potential Energy
▣ 5.4 Conservation of Energy
Q11. State the law of conservation of energy.
Answer:  Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it changes form. Total energy of an isolated system remains constant: KE + PE = constant (when only conservative forces act).
⚡ Shortcut:  Top: PE max, KE=0. Bottom: KE max, PE=0. Total constant.
Example:  A falling object: mgh at top = ½mv² at bottom.
Q12. Find the speed of a body falling from 80 m (from rest).
⚡ Shortcut:  v = √(2gh).
Example:  ≈ 40 m/s just before impact.
Q13. Explain energy changes in a simple pendulum.

Answer:  At the extreme positions height (and PE) is maximum and speed (KE) is zero; at the lowest point KE is maximum and PE is minimum. Total mechanical energy stays constant (ignoring air resistance).
⚡ Shortcut:  PE ↔ KE, total constant.
Example:  Swing is fastest at the bottom.
▥ 5.4 Conservation of Energy  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Mechanical Energy: When Is it Conserved?
▣ 5.5 Conservative & Non-conservative Forces; Collisions
Q14. Define conservative and non-conservative forces with examples.

Answer:  Conservative forces: work is path-independent and total work around a closed loop is zero (gravity, spring, electrostatic). Non-conservative: work depends on path, converts energy to other forms (friction, air resistance).
⚡ Shortcut:  Gravity/spring = conservative; friction = non-conservative.
Example:  Sliding down a rough incline loses mechanical energy to heat.
Q15. Distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions.

Answer:  Elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved (e.g. ideal gas molecules). Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved but KE is not (part converts to heat/sound); perfectly inelastic bodies stick together.
⚡ Shortcut:  Elastic: KE conserved. Inelastic: KE lost. Momentum conserved in both.
Example:  Billiard balls ≈ elastic; car crashes are inelastic.
Q16. In a perfectly inelastic collision, is momentum or kinetic energy conserved?
Answer:  Momentum is conserved (no external force). Kinetic energy is not conserved; some is converted to heat, sound and deformation. The bodies move with a common final velocity.
⚡ Shortcut:  Inelastic: Σp conserved, KE not.
Example:  Two clay balls stick together and slow down.
Q17. Coefficient of restitution e. What is e for elastic and perfectly inelastic collision?
Answer:  e = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach. For an elastic collision e = 1; for a perfectly inelastic collision (bodies stick) e = 0.
⚡ Shortcut:  e=1 elastic; e=0 perfectly inelastic; 0<e<1 partially.
Example:  Rubber ball has higher e than a clay ball.

▹ Derive  (derivations & long answers)
[Derive] T1. Derive the work-energy theorem.
Answer:  Net work = ma×s = ma(v²−u²)/2a = ½m(v²−u²) = ΔKE. So W_net = change in kinetic energy, regardless of the forces involved.
⚡ Short / exam line:  W_net = ΔKE = ½m(v²−u²).
Example:  A force speeding a body up stores the work as KE.
[Derive] T2. Derive the energy stored in a stretched spring (elastic potential energy).
Answer:  Work = area under the F–x graph; for Hooke's law F = kx this is a triangle: U = ½·F·Δx = ½kx². Energy density = ½(stress)(strain).
⚡ Short / exam line:  U = ½kx² = ½Fx.
Example:  A 100 N over 0.1 m stores 5 J.
▹ State  (definitions, laws & formulae)
[State] T3. Define work, kinetic energy and potential energy with units.
Answer:  Work = force × displacement along the force (J). KE = ½mv² (J) – energy of motion. PE (grav) = mgh (J) – energy of position. All in joules.
⚡ Short / exam line:  W=Fs ; KE=½mv² ; PE=mgh.
Example:  A lifted 10 kg at 2 m → PE = 196 J.
[State] T4. State the law of conservation of energy and apply it to a falling body.
Answer:  Energy is neither created nor destroyed; it changes form. A body falling from rest: mgh at the top = ½mv² at the bottom, so v = √(2gh).
⚡ Short / exam line:  mgh ↔ ½mv² (free fall).
Example:  Drop 5 m → v = √(98) ≈ 9.9 m/s.
▹ Compare  (compare & contrast)
[Compare] T5. Compare elastic and inelastic collisions (with coefficient of restitution).
Answer:  Elastic: both momentum and KE conserved, e = 1 (ideal gas, billiard). Inelastic: momentum conserved but KE lost, e < 1; perfectly inelastic (bodies stick), e = 0, maximum KE lost.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Elastic e=1; perfectly inelastic e=0.
Example:  Car crash = inelastic; pool balls ≈ elastic.
▹ Explain  (working / principle / application)
[Explain] T6. Explain the work-energy theorem's application in braking.
Answer:  The braking (friction) force does negative work equal to the loss in KE: W = −½mv². The work dissipated is converted to heat in the brakes; this fixes the minimum stopping distance.
⚡ Short / exam line:  W_brake = −KE → heat.
Example:  Stopping a car converts KE into thermal energy.
[Explain] T7. Explain conservative and non-conservative forces with examples.

Answer:  Conservative (gravity, spring, electrostatic): work depends only on end points, zero around a closed loop, and a potential energy can be defined. Non-conservative (friction, air drag): work depends on path, converts mechanical energy to heat, no potential energy.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Gravity = conservative; friction = non-conservative.
Example:  Sliding down a rough ramp loses energy to heat.
▹ Why  (conceptual & 'why' questions)
[Why] T8. Why is the total energy of a bound system negative?
Answer:  Because zero energy is set at infinite separation; since binding holds the system together, its total energy lies below that zero, i.e. negative. Unbound systems have E ≥ 0.
⚡ Short / exam line:  E_total < 0 → bound; = 0 threshold; > 0 unbound.
Example:  A satellite in orbit has negative total energy.
▹ Numerical  (long numericals / problems)
[Numerical] T9. A 1500 kg car travels at 30 m/s and stops in 5 s. Find the average braking force and distance.
⚡ Short / exam line:  F=ma; s=u²/2|a|.
Example:  75 m stopping distance; 9 kN force.
